Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette:
Aisha was twenty years old when she was deployed to a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan, a database administrator whose job was supposed to be safe-maintaining personnel records and supply logs from inside a reinforced container. She had been there for three weeks when a mortar round struck the perimeter wall thirty yards from her workstation. The blast threw her chair sideways; she landed on her shoulder, and for what felt like minutes she lay on the concrete floor, ears ringing, unable to move, certain the next round would land on her. No one came for her. She crawled to a corner and stayed there, pressing herself into the seam where the floor met the wall, until someone finally opened the door and shouted that it was over.

Now, a year and a half later, Aisha is back in the United States, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment in Dearborn, Michigan, and working remotely for a logistics company. She has become meticulous about her environment in ways that her coworkers and family find puzzling. Every evening, before she can sit down to eat dinner, she must wipe down the kitchen counters with bleach spray, then arrange the bottles in the cabinet by height, labels facing forward. If she skips this routine, she finds herself unable to focus, her chest tightening until she goes back and does it properly. She has come to believe that order in her immediate surroundings is the only thing she can control, and that without it, something terrible will happen-though she cannot say what.

Aisha no longer goes outside after dark. The first time she tried, a few months after returning home, she walked to the corner store to buy milk and found herself frozen on the sidewalk, her heart hammering, convinced that a car backfiring was the start of an attack. She turned around and walked home without the milk, and since then she has simply stopped trying. She orders groceries online, schedules all her meetings during daylight hours, and if a friend invites her to dinner after sunset, she declines without explanation. Her coworkers assume she is antisocial; her mother thinks she is depressed. Aisha does not correct them.

She also avoids anything that puts her body under stress. She stopped going to the gym because the feeling of being out of breath reminded her of the moment after the blast, when she could not get enough air. She no longer jogs, even in the daytime. She walks slowly, deliberately, keeping her breathing shallow and even, and if she has to climb stairs she takes them one at a time, pausing at each landing. She knows this is not normal for someone her age, but she is certain that if she lets herself get winded, she will panic and not be able to stop.

What finally brought Aisha to seek help was a moment at work last week. She was on a video call with her supervisor when the fire alarm went off in her building-a routine test, she later learned-but for three full seconds she could not speak, could not move, could only stare at the camera while her supervisor said her name repeatedly. She ended the call without explanation and spent the next hour cleaning her bathroom, scrubbing the grout between the tiles until her fingers were raw. That night, she sent an email to a therapist who specialized in trauma. She does not know if talking about it will help. What she is most afraid of is that the therapist will tell her she has to go outside after dark, or stop cleaning, or start running again. But she is also afraid of staying exactly where she is.
